content:
Handling cybercrime isn’t just about making a quick decision—it is about accurately identifying the problem and finding the right solution in time.
Recently, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has become directly involved in investigating "digital arrest" scams and is taking strict action against them. If you are a victim, have lost money, or are being threatened, immediately dial 1930 (the National Cyber Crime Helpline) or visit your nearest police station to verify the facts.
Do not trust documents sent online claiming you are a culprit or an accused person. Instead, pause and take your time. Legally, there is no such thing as a "digital arrest." Scammers deliberately create a sense of fear and urgency to cloud your critical thinking, pressuring you into transferring money before you have a chance to verify the truth.
Today, law enforcement agencies are taking strict legal action against these syndicates under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS):
• Cheating and Forgery: FIRs are being registered under Section 318(4) (cheating) as well as Sections 336, 337, and 338 (forgery of documents and valuable securities).
• Organized Crime: When an organized syndicate or a "mule" bank account holder is identified, police are booking them under Section 111 for organized crime.
• Criminal Conspiracy: If individuals are found plotting or executing a coordinated conspiracy against a victim, they are charged under Sections 61 and 62 alongside other relevant criminal acts.
comment: One practical challenge is preserving the money trail. Victims often delay reporting out of fear, while rapid coordination with banks can make the difference between tracing funds and losing them across multiple mule accounts.
